Whereas figures released today by the Department of Finance indicate that Canada's foreign reserves have fallen by $573 million since the end of last year, and whereas those same figures indicate that our U.S. dollar reserves have declined by $565 million while the Canadian dollar has fallen to a 95-cent range, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Ritchie):

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege, and do not do so lightly, and do not do so in this House at all frequently. It pertains to what has become the persistent practice of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) to ignore his serious responsibilities to the House of Commons and, therefore, directly to the people of Canada.

subtopic: MR BROADBENT-FAILURE OF MINISTER OF TRANSPORT TO MAKE POLICY STATEMENTS IN HOUSE OF COMMONS

Members of this House do not object if ministers make statements outside the House infrequently on minor matters of policy, but when a minister of the Crown, twice within a period of 72 hours, deliberately ignores parliament-I will explain why 1 say he deliberately ignores parliament and make that point clear in a second-when he made a major statement in British Columbia, 48 hours ago, on transportation policy concerning passenger services primarily, and this afternoon he is scheduled, not in another province or at a distance but in Ottawa, to have a press conference at which he is going to announce another major policy decision of the government of Canada, then we object. This time it affects another significant part of our transportation system, and in both cases hundreds of millions of dollars of taxpayers money are involved.
In both cases major policy alternatives have presumably been considered by the government and normally would be commented upon by opposition parties on this side of the House. Therefore 1 say that the minister is systematically avoiding his responsibilities to the House-two days ago in Vancouver and today in Ottawa-by making announcements of government policy outside the House.
What can be the reason for this, Mr. Speaker? The only reason is that the minister is trying to manipulate the news media; the only reason is that the minister knows that if he makes a statement on policy outside the House of Commons he is directly accountable to no one and he is not questioned here in the House.
The reply by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) to a question near the end of the question period, in which it was seriously suggested that the Prime Minister exercise his responsibility by directing the Minister of Transport to make his 3.30 p.m. announcement here in the House instead of across the street was, to put it mildly, deplorable.

Order, please. The hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broadbent) has raised, by way of a question of privilege, the failure of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) to make important announcements concerning national transportation policy in the House of Commons. He has asked that if the Chair finds a case has been established that the question be put to the House as to whether that failure ought to form the substance of a motion of referral of the failure to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections.
It has been clear, and the hon. member clearly understood and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) just pointed out, that there is a total absence of authority to be enforced by the Chair, or in the regulations of the House, to compel the minister to make a statement, just as there is a total absence of authority to compel an answer to be given by a minister during question period for the reason that the satisfaction of that kind of compulsory order would be most difficult to define and describe.
However, the question that is before me now is not whether it is preferable that the minister make such a statement or statements in the House, or preferable that parliament be
March 2, 1977

given priority in respect to the making of these statements over press conferences.
The question before me is whether or not, within the definition of questions of privilege, the failure of a minister, either now or at any time, or the action of a minister in choosing to make a statement outside the House instead of inside the House, can ever constitute a question of privilege within the definition as we know it.
There is a tendency to refer to the establishment of a prima facie case of privilege. With respect, I think that that language is slightly misleading. What really is being sought is the action of the Chair in agreeing to withhold the putting of other questions or taking of other business in order to put the question which is moved, or which would be moved, as a priority matter, giving it that special priority because it relates to the privileges, either individually or collectively, of members of this House. Therefore the question for the Chair is: does this question so fundamentally relate to the privileges of the members of the House, within the definition of privilege as we know it, that it ought to enjoy immediate priority and that the Chair ought to put the question forthwith for a decision by the House?
The precedents are directly against that in respect to the actions of ministers in choosing, as they are of course entitled to do at any time. It is not appropriate for the Chair to make any comment on whether that is preferable. The only question is whether the minister has a discretion to choose to make statements outside or inside the House.
Not only is it clear that any minister would enjoy that discretion, in fact the language of the Standing Order says particularly that, when the procedures of the Standing Order are to be taken advantage of, a minister of the Crown may make a statement inside the House. That is the language that is used. His discretion, therefore, is not only, as always, to take whatever action he wants outside the House; the discretion even is one of an option for the minister to use the House for that purpose.
There is no need to repeat the language of the precedents. We did that when the matter has been raised previously. The language of the precedents is very clear. Nothing in the Standing Orders in any way interferes with the minister's discretion. The point, I think, has been fully amplified. It has been well and thoroughly discussed. It does not in any way change the precedent.
I should add one other matter. Although it does not constitute a question of privilege and therefore enjoy priority, that is not to say that the motion cannot be put forward in other ways, this or any other motion criticizing any act of a member.
Sometimes when such motions do not qualify within the four corners of a question of privilege, there is a tendency to believe the House is rejecting them out of hand. That is not the case. There are other ways of bringing motions before the House. A question of privilege gives a motion very special priority and, therefore, is defined within very narrow limits. Within those

narrow limits I must find that the conditions of privilege have not been met in this particular instance.

The precedents to be referred to, as to whether or not that constitutes a sufficient quoting or citing of a document to demand the tabling of it, are clearly recorded at page 2441 of Hansard for January 27 of this year. Again 1 would refer to the very clear and explicit language used by my predecessor, which is always of great assistance:
In fairness, looking at the matter as objectively as I can, I do not see how it is possible for the Chair to make a ruling at this point that a document which has simply been referred to but has not been directly quoted should be tabled in debate.

speechtext: Are mountain climbing parties in Kluanc National Park required to (a) obtain a permit for the expedition (b) apply for a permit three months in advance (c) have at least four members (d) provide a complete list of members (c) furnish medical certificates, signed by a doctor, for each member (f) provide a complete itinerary (g) provide a complete list of personal and community equipment (h) appear at a ranger station for personal inspection (i) identify blood type for each member (j) possess a radio to call for help, or arrange for a regular aircraft flyby and. if so, in each case, for what reason?

speakeroldname: Mr. B. Keith Penner (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subsubtopic: MOUNTAIN CLIMBING-KLUANE NATIONAL PARK
speechtext:
Requirements for mountain climbing parties in Kluane National Park are set out in Section 23 of the National Parks Act. (a) Yes. Climbers must check in and out with the Park Warden Service when attempting a climb of any difficulty. Control is achieved by issuing permits, (b) No. This is a guideline, (c) No. This is a guideline, (d) Yes. This is for control purposes. Members are named on permit so park management knows exactly who is on the mountain, (e) No. This is a guideline. (0 Yes. In the event that rescue operations are necessary, this information would provide a starting point in search efforts, (g) No. This is a guideline, (h) There is no need to appear at Park Warden stations. This is a guideline, (i) No. This is a guideline, (j) No. This is a guideline. Depending on the degree of the climb, different degrees of preparedness are encouraged. All climbers are urged to adhere as fully as they can to the guidelines, but for the most severe climbs, such as Mount Logan, all of the guidelines should be adhered to. The primary purpose is concern for the safety of the climbing party. Following these guidelines aids in the prevention of costly and, in many cases, dangerous search and rescue operations.

Mr. Speaker, 1 raise this question on the first opportunity I have been given to raise it. My question may be a question of privilege relating to the growing trend of the government's to give either not correct answers or not factual answers in respect of questions placed on the order paper.
On November 18 last, if my memory serves me right, I placed a simple question on the order paper relating to the total amount of money going from the government to the province of Quebec and the total amount coming back from the province of Quebec to this government. Yesterday, Sir, 1 received an answer to this question, an answer from the government, stating that such information was not available. Coincidentally, last night when I watched the CTV television news there appeared a program giving exactly that type of information I had requested.
On inquiring of the CTV news, I learned that the information had emanated from Maclean's magazine which, in turn, had obtained the information from the government. Sir, I put myself entirely in your hands, because I do not know how further to proceed. Is it not a question of privilege when a member of parliament, using acknowledged and correct procedures to obtain information from the government, is refused that information and finds that the media can get exactly the same information far more easily than he can? Is that not a question of privilege, Sir?

speechtext: The House resumed, from Tuesday, March 1, consideration of the motion of Mr. Basford (for the Minister of Transport) that Bill C-33, to amend the National Transportation Act and the Department of Transport Act for the purpose of defining the objective of the transportation policy of Canada and authorizing the consequential rearrangement of powers and duties relating to transport and to amend the Transport Act and the Railway Act in respect of freight rates and other matters, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO REDEFINE OBJECTIVE OF TRANSPORTATION POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when I interrupted my remarks last night to call it ten o'clock I had made a few preliminary remarks about Bill C-33. There are three main objectives-definition, authority, and improvement. I said transportation was a top priority, that it was a huge, difficult and urgent one, just like finding oil. I said this bill was worth supporting and I felt I could support it, depending upon what kind of general acceptance it found in its passage through the House, and upon what chances there were of its provisions being carried out.
There is, however, a logical progress of events, and I think this support has to be conditional upon something. It has to be conditional upon the fact that there are some election campaign promises already on the books which have not been fulfilled to the satisfaction of many people. In other words, first things first.
The national transportation program which has been outlined in some detail since 1974 is, in my view, an excellent program especially for the long term, but it really needs a strong short term start, something it does not appear to have. There are many advantages attached to this program, with its objective of providing better, cheaper, and more energy efficient transportation, giving Canadian industry a boost in the transport field ajid giving the economy a general boost. But besides transport there is this other issue-the business of honouring commitments, the business of keeping election promises, the business of the integrity and the credibility of government. In my opinion it is not good enough to say with regard to a top priority operation like transport that there is not enough money now.
March 2, 1977

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO REDEFINE OBJECTIVE OF TRANSPORTATION POLICY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO REDEFINE OBJECTIVE OF TRANSPORTATION POLICY
speechtext:
It is not good enough to say this is not our business, that it is the business of the provinces and the municipalities. If this is important, then it is important to find the money, and if the Canadian people see this as their business, and if they want it to be the business of the federal government, we have an obligation to make it our business.
It is difficult to pin these promises down in terms of exact amounts. It seems to me something was mentioned about $300 million for five years for the entire transportation program, one third of which was to be available in the form of financial aid to commuter systems. Well, Mr. Speaker, this is really a drop in the bucket. It may seem a lot of money, but it is certainly not a lot in relation to the transportation needs of the whole country. The Toronto area alone needs $50 million just for starters-half the total amount mentioned. If there is anything with which I would disagree in relation to the campaign promises in this field, if there was one mistake, it was the open-ended cost-sharing provision. I think this is one part of the promise which the federal government could feel justified in breaking. It is the type of nonsensical thing we have been trying to get away from in medicare, and hospital care. We know the temptation is just too great. It simply does not work. But there is no reason why we cannot come up with a decent amount of money within a stipulated time frame.
The type of commitment which was made in terms of open cost-sharing-to the extent of 100 per cent for commuter rolling stock, 50 per cent for platforms and supporting structures, and 25 per cent for inner city transit-is obviously unrealistic. We have had some discussion about this, and one of the stipulations we would make in this connection is that all the equipment and all the machinery be made in Canada. Another was that there be a limited time frame, thus providing an opportunity to reassess the program-in other words, the budget would not get out of hand. Finally, due credit was to be given for the contribution of each level of government, including the federal government. This should not be a problem; we all want credit for what we do. Up until now it does seem to have been a problem in terms of the levels of government not getting along together.
The reasons given by ministers for restricting this program, perhaps for even cancelling it, are as follows: first, restraint. We believe in restraint. The caucus has been urging it on the government for two and a half years. The government seems, finally, to be doing a good job of it. But the question is: where should restraint be applied? Second, as I mentioned before, there is the business of jurisdiction and political games-a lack of credit for what is done.
Some have asked is there a federal role for urban transit? Why not? Certainly the federal government has assumed a role in urban housing. And there are other areas. If the provinces do not want that kind of support from the federal government they are free to refuse it.
There was an original premise built into this program, Mr. Speaker, and many people realized this. This was not just a
National Transportation Act
way to spend money. This was not supposed to be throwing money down the drain. This whole transport program, besides being important in itself, was designed both to save and to make money by providing cheaper, more efficient transportation. Those things have to be taken into account when we talk of cancelling the program or restraining it. It does not sound as though they were taken into account. Against this is the cost of supporting air travel and private transportation as we have done up to now.
The costs of infrastructure at airports, and the upkeep and construction of roads and super highways, parking lots and all the rest are enormous. Surely there is money to be saved there which could be put into a better transportation program?
What about a possible tie-in with Canada Works? The opportunity exists in a transportation program to provide jobs. But in this case, if there is a public transit industry, we should provide real jobs, not makeshift jobs. Corporations under Canada Works are allowed to sponsor projects; why not projects concerning public transit? Presumably there is an opportunity to spend money there. I suppose this will require a budgetary exercise, a complete rearranging of our priorities and expenditures, looking outside transportation into other departments.
I heard recently that we may be planning to spend $2.5 billion on jet fighters. To my mind there is no question what are the priorities at the present time. I am all for adequate defence and support for the military, but good public transport comes first, in my opinion.
Perhaps we will have to take another look at our social and welfare programs and ask whether there are some unnecessary expenses involved, especially in regard to universality of payments, which means paying benefits to people who do not need them, to people who are wealthy and can get along without them. Perhaps there is money to be saved in limiting the bureaucracy, the size of the civil service. I think it is timely to think in terms of rearranging our budget priorities since we will soon be dealing with the main estimates. I think they are a little hard for the average MP to understand, but none the less we can tie this subject into them. Also we have a spring budget coming up which is designated to stimulate the economy.
There is a temptation, Mr. Speaker, for some people to think that the public and the media are not interested in this subject, that it will go away by itself. On the contrary, there have been a flurry of reports in the media and it is the number one subject of talk in my riding, and I imagine in many others. There have been many calls from reporters for interviews even of lowly backbenchers. For example, the Milton Champion reports that Milton definitely needs an extension of the Go train system but that federal funds had been withdrawn and Go train plans shelved. I know that will lead to a lot of disappointment. The Globe and Mail reported that Liberal MP's were considering a revolt over transit cuts. I think that is a little bit over-dramatic but it indicates the kind of feelings that have been generated.

March 2, 1977
National Transportation Act
Local Halton people are almost unanimously urging support for this program; I have heard no one speak against it. Telegrams from local politicians have been entirely in support of this transit program. I have received a telegram from Halton regional chairman, Rick Morrow, as well as from Burlington mayor, Mary Munro. Let me just read the telegram from Rick Morrow:
Wish to express serious concern regarding announced withdrawal of federal funds for urban transit. Will seriously affect planned extension of Go servicing to Milton, Oakville and Burlington. Request use of your office to seek government reconsideration of the matter.
"Ottawa Makes Chaos for Commuters" reports the Toronto Daily Star for February 22, 1977. The members for Halton (Mr. Philbrook) and Mississauga (Mr. Abbott) were cited as not helping, but that is incorrect and I think has subsequently been corrected. The Oakville paper, the Journal Record, carried the headline "Federal Transit Aid Delayed, Not Dead: Philbrook"; that was certainly a high hope in the determination. "The transit program has been curtailed due to restraint", said the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) in a recent Toronto interview. The Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) is reported by the Ottawa Citizen for February 24 as saying that the "onus is on others for transit". Then just at the end of last week the Globe and Mail attributes the headline "Transit Support Plan Still Before Cabinet" to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). So maybe we have a life yet.
We need many modes of transportation in this country, and we need them urgently. We need them for many parts of the country. We need faster intercity rail, not only for the Quebec City-Windsor corridor but for many other parts of the country, such as from Calgary to Edmonton and so on. Most of all, we need a lot of help for the maritimes, because they tend to be neglected. Then what about Newfoundland and the old "Bullet"? And let us not forget the prairie services.
Perhaps we also need plans to develop the controversial STOL aircraft for outlying cities, because what else is there? The people themselves say that trains and buses are not sufficient, and that is certainly correct if we want to decentralize and relieve urban crowding. We need better intercity transit for our urban areas, and we certainly need a much better freight deal to help solve our western grain and port problems.
I come from a suburban area, one of many in Canada. Perhaps there are 25 major areas like mine, and my particular interest is commuter transit in trying to convey people back and forth between suburbs and cities in a decent, civilized manner. Some people say there should be no problem, that people should live where they work, but I think at the moment that is a little unrealistic and will take a long time to bring about. Until this happens, we must look after these people. We need more Go trains now; we cannot delay such decisions because we do not want to bother changing the budget. Most of all, we need less emphasis on what we have had a bellyfull of in the last generation, namely, too much air travel.
Out Halton way-and this also applies to my colleague for Mississauga-we need $15 million fast to relieve terrible
[Mr. Philbrook.J
congestion, and I am sorry to say that this is half of the entire amount budgeted for the next five years for commuter transit. We need this money for Go trains and for extra rolling stock. We need additional Go train service to a place like Milton, which is virtually isolated despite the fact it is near a big city, not new Go buses. Improvements are required to Union Station to facilitate arrival and departure. We must relieve the bottleneck at the Bathurst Street crossing. We need improved trackage and, as I say, additional cars. The Ontario government and the Toronto city council have made commitments to spend money for this purpose, to the best of my knowledge, and the political lesson of this step has not been lost on them. If we do not come through and meet this requirement, we are going to be very, very sorry.
With all due respect to my party and my leader, Mr. Speaker, there is no doubt in my mind that my main responsibility is to my constituents at this moment. This responsibility of mine is closely related to the improvement of nation-wide transit and to campaign promises. Even our opponents in provincial and municipal governments have made commitments in this regard. They have stuck their necks out and are now left holding the bag, being faced with a great deal of expenditure.
I am prepared to support this bill, but this is certainly contingent on some kind of tangible evidence coming to light very soon that the government is prepared to follow through on its campaign promises to improve transportation. I would invite my colleagues to take the same stand.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO REDEFINE OBJECTIVE OF TRANSPORTATION POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
I welcome the opportunity to speak on Bill C-33 this afternoon, to amend the National Transportation Act and the Department of Transport Act for the purpose of defining the objective of the transportation policy for Canada, and authorizing the consequential rearrangement of powers and duties relating to transport and to amend the Transport Act and the Railway Act in respect of freight rates and other matters.
It is interesting to note that proposed section 3(2)(d) provides that "competition within and between modes of transportation should be encouraged where economic and technical factors permit". I have nothing against competition. I am going to refer to the trucking industry of Canada, particularly in Manitoba, and to the problems the government is laying on Manitoba's doorstep at the present time with the introduction by the Post Office of their new postpak delivery service, which I suggest will unfairly compete with the trucking industry. I will go into that in more detail in just a moment. In subclause (3)(a) in the bill dealing with the minister's responsibilities it is stated:
[DOT] (noo)
-inquire into and undertake measures to ensure the effective and inefficient development of the various forms of transport over which parliament has jurisdiction;
With the introduction of the postpak delivery service we are certainly not going to have an effective and efficient development of various modes of transport, especially in the trucking
March 2, 1977

industry. This postpak concept has been introduced recently by the Post Office. It is a new concept for moving merchandise from coast to coast. It is a mini container system using the mailbags to move goods in bulk. Mailbags can carry up to 66 pounds.
A couple of years ago the government commissioned a study costing a quarter of a million dollars on the difference in deliveries between the Post Office providing its own trucks, and prfvate industry. This Samson Belair study contained recommendations, facts, and figures showing why all mail delivery should be left to the private sector because the savings would amount to millions of dollars. Unfortunately this detailed study and research were completely ignored, and the Post Office took over postal delivery and set up its own trucking system.
In the last parliament I tried to obtain a copy of this Samson Belair document but the government refused to table it. Fortunately I was able to obtain it. This study should have been referred to one of the standing committees discussing Post Office operations for a complete and detailed study and review of the recommendations made in it. I would like to read some of the recommendations in the report. It reads:
In future the department should contract for city services unless there is conclusive evidence as to the unavailability of this service on reasonable terms from outside the department.
The present government operations should be reviewed with the objective of securing the services outside. Potential savings from the conversion of the four existing government operations would amount to approximately $725,000 per year.
What they are saying is that it would be $725,000 a year cheaper to let a private trucking company handle postal deliveries. How such a recommendation could possibly have been ignored has never been explained. Now we find that the Post Office has come up with this postpak proposal which is causing no end of problems to the trucking industry, as I will explain in more detail in a few minutes.
The Samson Belair report goes on to say:
The department should review all other government performed transportation and distribution services to determine whether new or increased needs could not be more satisfactorily performed by the private sector.
The study goes on to say:
Considering only direct field costs, the four existing government operated urban services are more costly than an equivalent contracted operation. Were other costs such as rent, administration, interest on capital, and taxes on such items as gasoline, purchases, and corporate income to be considered, the argument for a contracted service would be further substantiated.
So you see there is no end of evidence as to why the Post Office should not have its own fleet to deliver mail. The additional cost is striking. What I am asking the minister to do this afternoon is to review this postpak proposal and consult the Postmaster General (Mr. Blais) with a view to disbanding this costly and unnecessary service being established by the Post Office at this time.
The report goes on to read:
Operational factors such as level of service, performance, control and flexibility associated with an effective contracted service are at least equivalent to a government operation.
National Transportation Act
The major factor in the cost gap between government and contracted services is labour productivity, and to a lesser extent administrative and supervisory costs.
The Samson Belair study stated that:
A contracted operation for this service is less costly than a government operation.
So it is less costly to leave to private truckers. It seems to be plain common sense to leave it to them. The study states further:
Payment on a point-of-call basis results in increased productivity and efficiency since the contractor is provided with an incentive to complete deliveries as early as possible.
Payment on a possible point-of-call basis is easier to administer because it eliminates the need to maintain a detailed record of hours worked by the contractor.
I will give you an example of what happened when the Post Office took over the mail delivery service and established its own fleet.
These are answers to questions on the Order Paper with which the government provided me. When the Post Office set up its own fleet in the city of Toronto, it required 44 more trucks than the private contractor needed for delivering the mail. It required 100 more employees than the private sector needed when it handled mail delivery in Toronto. The city of Montreal needed 10 more trucks and 160 more men when the Post Office set up its own delivery service. In the city of London, Ontario, 19 more trucks and 18 more men were needed. In Hamilton it took 15 more trucks to handle mail delivery and 17 more men. In the Kitchener-Waterloo area 8 more trucks were needed and 7 more men were needed to handle mail delivery. You can see the fantastic additional costs.
The ironic part of all this is that this is the point at which the quality of the service started to deteriorate. In my riding there is a large area of small businesses. Prior to the time when the Post Office handled its own deliveries the businessmen could set their clock by the time when the private mail contractor would come around with the mail each day. After the Post Office set up its own operation in Winnipeg, the businessmen never knew when the mail was coming, and yet the Post Office employs many more men and uses many more trucks.
There was an article in the Manitoba Highway News dated February, 1977, dealing with the problems that the new postpak is causing in Manitoba. They have carried out a detailed study of this and they are continuing to study the matter. I should like to quote from an article headed "Post Office Now in the Trucking Business. Big Deficit Seen?" The article reads:
Not content with acquiring a deficit of over half a billion dollars during the past year, the Post Office department has embarked on a scheme whereby, without too much more effort on their part, the bill the next time around could reach the billion dollar mark.
A great part of this will come through the postpak idea which started several years ago with a great fanfare of superior service and much lower cost than the established services being held out to the shipping public.
Low rates were established because the shipper had to be responsible for delivery to the Post Office and prepay all shipments which could consist of up to

March 2, 1977
National Transportation Act
50 lbs. in bags supplied by the Post Office or cartons of certain sizes and standards up to 66 lbs. In cities over 10,000 population delivery would be made by the P.O., otherwise the customer would be phoned. Delivery was to be similar to first class mail service. However, we find that it has been admitted that, under certain circumstances, the P.O. would also pick up at shippers' premises the postpak shipments. The development of this service can have a very serious impact on the truck service presently being provided by the regular over-the-road carrier as many small points have no other means of transport than the truck carrier on a regular basis.
Two main complaints arise from this operation. First, the trucker should not have to face a competitor that has access to the public purse to meet any deficits.
They will certainly be coming to the public purse to meet deficits with regard to this Postpak proposal, as shown by the other evidence I had read into the record this afternoon.
The trucker has no such access. Secondly, they should not have to compete with a delivery service by private contractors to the Post Office that are not required to meet the same standards as the licensed carrier. The Postpak system is said to bypass the ordinary P.O. procedures but does not require to move under bills of lading, or other terms and conditions as required by provincial regulatory boards. Labour regulations, either provincial or federal, are not required. The present licence fees for a truck hauling mail in Manitoba with a gross weight of 24,000 lbs. is as follows: based on a 1974 model truck, the fee would be $107.00, including insurance with $200.00 deductible all perils. For a semi-trailer carrying up to 80,000 lbs. the fee is $196.00 with no mileage limit. The regular line haul P.S.V. operator is required to pay $637.00 for an equivalent weight with a $500.00 deductible coverage. For the semi-trailer with 80,000 lbs. the fees would be $978.00 based on 1976 regulations.
Hon. members can see that this service should be provided by private truckers who are faced with these heavy licence fees; the government should not be coming out with this postpak proposal to hinder them and cause them more problems. We have enough problems with our sagging economy and so forth without the Post Office competing with private trucking companies.
The article continues as follows:
This problem has been brought to the attention of the various motor carrier boards in Canada and action has been requested to correct this inequity. However, it seems that most provinces are afraid to challenge the rights of the Post Office and, as a result, very little has been accomplished. At the present time the Canadian Trucking Association, through its national provincial standards council, is actively pursuing a course of action which we hope will bring some results.
Another activity of the Post Office is the lowering of charges on fourth class parcels. Recently they advertised in Winnipeg that they would guarantee next day delivery on fourth class parcels up to a weight of 35 lbs. This delivery was to be to any post office south of Lynn Lake, which is 600 miles north of Winnipeg.
The charge for a two-pound parcel was to be, for a distance of up to 150 miles, 60c.
Hon. members can see that taxpayers are going to be subsidizing this postpak delivery service which has been set up by the Post Office.
The article goes on:
On enquiring at the Post Office as to how many hands this parcel would go through before reaching its destination, it was said that six people would handle it! It would then be transported by air, if necessary, and delivered. Other weights were comparable.
Can hon. members imagine all this for 60 cents, six people handling it? It will be going by truck and by air. What a ridiculous proposal! The article goes on:
Efficiency plus: a tender has just been called for the furnishing of two one-ton trucks to provide service between Winnipeg and Thunder Bay. We wonder why, [Mr. McKenzie.)
when there are several airflights each day. at least four buses and five truck lines per day.
Now we find that the government is going to provide two more trucks, when all it has to do is contract mail delivery and parcel delivery out to bus companies or to the five truck lines which run to Thunder Bay. How ridiculous can the government get?
Here we are discussing a bill to make it easier and better for transportation businesses in the country, and the government comes out with a proposal like this which will cause no end to competitive problems and unfair competition. The article goes on:
Maybe it's time that the opposition at Ottawa started asking questions about Post Office operations in this area.
That is the only part of the article I do not agree with, because the hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale) and other hon. members on this side have certainly asked many questions about the Post Office, and I have certainly pursued Post Office problems in the last parliament and in this one. The article concludes by saying the following:
Is it any wonder that Post Office deficits in the neighbourhood of a billion dollars are believable?
When I obtained my copy of the Samson Belair study on postal operations and on whether mail delivery should be left in the hands of private trucking companies, I obtained information with regard to the number of additional trucks and employees which will be needed when the Post Office establishes its own trucking service, and I raised this matter in the standing committee. I presented a motion that we review the report and conduct a study as to why it will take 44 additional trucks to deliver mail in Toronto and so forth, but my motion was defeated. I remember the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin) being at that committee meeting, and he was very emphatic in saying that he did not want to conduct any investigation into this ridiculous and costly operation. That is why I said no to him last night when he was making his mundane speech on transportation and explaining why hon. members of the New Democratic Party support the government's getting into the trucking business and why they will not allow an investigation into the costly operation of the Post Office.
In closing, I ask the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang), and the Postmaster General (Mr. Blais), to get their heads together with a view to closing down this postpak proposal and to stop putting all these obstacles in front of the private trucking companies of Manitoba and of Canada.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO REDEFINE OBJECTIVE OF TRANSPORTATION POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with great pleasure that I speak on this bill to amend the National Transportation Act because essentially transportation represents the history of this country. The history of Canada is the history of transportation. An area which is so large that it stretches from ocean to ocean has to be linked together one way or another. If we go back 200 or 300 years to the first movement of goods by canoe or by pack, we will see how integrally transportation of goods and people was part of the history of Canada.
March 2, 1977

The bill we have before us is basically a good bill. I agree with its thrust. The implementation of the National Transportation Act in 1967 and the creation of the Canadian Transport Commission created a number of problems. Too often parliament has set up an agency or a Crown corporation to operate the policies approved by parliament, and these agencies, Crown corporations or commissions become very removed from the day to day policy direction which should be followed.
Events change rapidly in our modern world, and acts such as the 1967 National Transportation Act have become impediments to the development of transportation goals in this country. I think transportation must be regarded as a tool of social development.
As 1 said, I basically support the thrust of the bill, but I have some grave reservations. My reservations are such that perhaps 1 will withhold my support from the bill. My arguments are basically similar to those put forward by my colleague, the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Philbrook). We are both concerned about urban transit, intercity transit, commuter trains, and the role of the federal government in these fields. Back in 1975-I think it was July of 1975-the then minister of transport, the Hon. Jean Marchand, tabled in this House three very impressive and well researched documents entitled, I believe, "A National Transportation Policy for Canada". They were in three parts. One dealt with movement of freight and commodities, one dealt with inter-city passenger service, and there was an over-all summary.
These documents represented years of well-thought-out research by the department and the government in an attempt to rationalize and come to grips with the transportation problems that affect this country. Nowhere in these documents, however, did we see any reference to potential federal government assistance to urban or commuter transit, and this is the main reason why 1 have great reservations about this particular bill.
Some people may say I am being intellectually dishonest to consider not supporting a bill to amend the National Transportation Act and the Department of Transport Act which does not really relate to federal assistance to urban and commuter transit. This argument is rubbish, Mr. Speaker. If we talk about federal assistance to urban and commuter transit, we do so in the context of a national transportation policy.
The bill before us is a good one; it is the keystone of the government's transportation policy and should be applauded. There may be those on the other side who lick their lips or howl in delight because supporters of the government decide they have reservations about a particular bill. I do not think they should put too much stock in the stand that I take, and 1 know I speak for the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Philbrook) in this. We are in no way nonsupportive of the government and its attempts to come to grips with the serious problems facing the country, whether they be problems of the economy or of national unity. We are 100 per cent behind the government. The fact that we are general supporters of the government,
National Transportation Act
however, does not mean to say we have to agree with every aspect of government policy. This is where I am making this particular distinction.
Transportation problems do not constitute a major issue, according to the Gallup poll. We have to realize that there are some people on the Hill and off the Hill who live by the Gallup poll alone. While transportation problems do not constitute a major issue for a majority of Canadians, nevertheless those people who live in our cities, in Toronto, Montreal, and Vancouver are concerned about the credibility of a government that makes promises that it fails to fulfil.
Let me be firm on one point, Mr. Speaker. The promises made to assist urban transit were unrealistic in the first place. It is questionable whether the federal government has the constitutional obligation to finance urban transit. Further, the promises implied that the federal government would involve itself in an open-ended funding program. This is precisely the position the government is trying to reverse with the recent agreement with the provinces on medicare. That is to say, the federal government has the obligation to encourage universal programs and standards across the country, and further it would and should encourage such programs and stapdards only for a fixed period of time.
There is no doubt that the federal government has the right to encourage the development of public transport for obvious reasons, such as land use planning, energy efficiency and net social cost. The question is how it should be done.
Let us look at some of the promises made by this party in the 1974 election campaign. I am sure the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) wishes there were no copies of this document left floating around the House of Commons, but I have a copy and I should like to put those promises on the record.
The government promised to pay 100 per cent of the cost of new commuter vehicles manufactured in Canada; to pay 50 per cent of the cost of new stations and platforms forming part of the system; to pay 25 per cent of the capital cost of all vehicles purchased each year for public transit within Canadian cities and which were manufactured in Canada. Financial support was to be made available to encourage Canadian design and engineering of top quality urban and suburban transit vehicles, systems, machinery and equipment. For smaller municipalities the government offered assistance not only in design, engineering, and financing, but in the form of expert advice in bringing new transit systems into operation. The government was determined to encourage Canadian industry to develop so-called "off the shelf' standardized systems and equipment, such as telebuses and urban commuter trains which could save the country millions of dollars in development costs and which would encourage Canadian transport designers, engineers, and manufacturers to become world leaders.
The government was to encourage urban transit system innovations, including further demonstration projects financed by the federal government. The government offered to make best use of existing railway rights of way and track in urban and suburban areas for new commuter and urban transit lines
3594

March 2, 1977
National Transportation Act
with a view to reducing the high cost of such systems to Canadian municipalities.
The government maintained it would rapidly implement the Railway Relocation Act to ensure that railway relocations in cities also contributed to the right kind of city growth.
Only a few of these promises were ever discharged, the most notable being one I have not read. The government was committed to removing the 12 per cent sales tax on all 12 passenger and up vehicles which would provide service as part of an urban transit system. This was done in the budget of 1975. It has helped municipalities considerably. The 12 per cent tax on large transit vehicles, such as the acquisition of subway cars in Toronto, or high speed street cars, amounts to a very large sum. I know the Toronto Transit Commission is particularly grateful, and I am sure most of the other municipal transit systems in Canada are grateful for the removal of this tax.
To recap, Mr. Speaker, the three main urban and commuter promises made by the government in 1974 were to pay 25 per cent of the capital cost of all Canadian made vehicles purchased by urban transit systems; to pay 100 per cent of the cost of new commuter vehicles such as the Go transit buses in Ontario; and to pay 50 per cent of the cost of new stations and platforms used by commuter systems.
The basic problem with these promises is their total cost and their implication of ongoing funding. With the need of the government to reduce its spending it is quite obvious that there just is not the money available to meet these promises in their entirety. Like my colleague, the hon. member for Halton, I have urged the government to restrain its spending and I think it has done a good job in curtailing expenditures in a difficult economic period.
The provinces and the cities do have an urgent need for financial assistance, however, and the federal government needs to restore some credibility with the public by going part way to discharge its promises. This then is the debate in which I am involved with the government: how much can we afford to do, and at what time should this assistance be given?
Let us take a closer look at the federal responsibility in urban and commuter transit. While it can be argued that the federal government does not have the constitutional obligation toward commuter services as such, the government has, over the past year, assumed a constitutional obligation toward directing growth away from cities-an obligation toward the demographic features of Canada and, to a lesser extent, toward a more socially conducive use of land resources. This can be seen in the conceptual approach to the new immigration act now before the House, for some of the reasons mentioned were given as the rationale for the new Immigration Act. Therefore the federal government has some obligation and moral jurisdiction in this area. I was talking about commuters a few minutes ago, Mr. Speaker.
Similarly, while the federal government has no constitutional jurisdiction in the matter of urban transport, it has a

constitutional obligation in the field of energy conservation, which includes an obligation towards Canadian industry and the creation of domestic job opportunities, in addition to its political obligations. Of course, speaking in purely political terms, we are obligated to help the municipalities and provinces.
Before I outline the extent of the commitment which would be appropriate for urban and commuter assistance, let me acknowledge that the government has made promises in the area of commuter assistance. There has been an ongoing program of assistance to provinces and municipalities with regard to urban and commuter transit.
Grants were first made available in the fiscal year 1972-73 for research and demonstration projects. About one year ago the government announced a program of capital assistance for various commuter projects. The first grants under this program are to be made on April 1, 1977. The purpose of the program is to assist provincial and municipal authorities to design and develop new technology, operations, innovations, etc. for urban transit. It is also to assist those authorities with the purchase of commuter vehicles and related facilities.
The provisions of these programs are as follows. Under the Department of Transport Act, the Transportation Development Agency may enter into agreements with provinces or municipalities to share the costs of transportation research over a set period of time. Besides providing financial support, the agency is to participate in the project, as a member of the steering committee. It is to monitor progress and provide advice and policy direction. In addition, under the capital assistance project for urban commuter services, grants will be made to provinces and municipalities to assist in the purchase of commuter vehicles and related facilities. The program will provide $100 million over five years, beginning April 1, 1977.
I contend that $100 million over five years, or $20 million a year, is not enough. My colleague from Halton suggested that the Go-transit system in Ontario needs to have an immediate $50 million spent on it, or about half the amount allotted for all of Canada. Clearly the government must make more money available for this program.
Let me now say a word about the achievements of programs designed to help municipalities and provinces in the field of commuter systems. From fiscal year 1972-73 to the end of the fiscal year 1975-76, a total of $1,233,900 was spend on research and demonstration projects. Projects were supported in Ontario, Quebec, the maritimes and each of the prairie provinces. Therefore it is incorrect to suggest that the government has not discharged the promises it made in 1974. The question is, to what extent has it discharged those promises and how much more should be done?

Oh, oh!
March 2, 1977

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO REDEFINE OBJECTIVE OF TRANSPORTATION POLICY
speechtext:
Recently the Ontario government has made several statements about our obligation to keep the promise we made with respect to aid to commuter systems. The minister of transport in Ontario said that the recent statement of the federal Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald), that our promises to help urban commuter transit were dead, would mean a complete halt to the expansion of the provincially operated Go-transit system. That system was to serve Milton, in the constituency of the hon. member for Halton, Richmond Hill, and the area north of Toronto lying in the constituency of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Danson). The minister in Ontario contends that this service cannot be expanded. That is absolute nonsense.
The improvement or expansion of the Go-transit system in and around Toronto depends upon improvements to Toronto's union station, better access to ticket offices, expansion of platforms, realignment of tracks in stations, and also on the reconstruction of the Bathurst Street bridge. At present there is a bottleneck at the Bathurst Street bridge. There is ongoing maintenance of passenger equipment, a lot of shunting in the areas and, in addition, heavy industry on the waterfront of Toronto. This industry must have access to general rail lines of downtown Toronto.
I must say that the number of tracks now going under the Bathurst Street bridge constitute a problem; the railways have told the province that the bridge must be rebuilt and more tracks laid in order to accommodate increased services. The question is, do these two projects, involving the improving of Union Station, ticket facilities and so on, and removing the bottleneck at the Bathurst Street bridge, come under the government's promised program to give capital assistance for the purchase of equipment? I say they do not.
There is a perfectly adequate program of grade separation which is implemented across the country. Under it we remove railroad tracks, or put railway tracks under roads, or build subways and have the tracks going over the road. I am sure that money could be found in the existing budget for the improvement of the Bathurst Street bottleneck. Similarly, it would not need an astronomical sum to improve Union Station and those other facilities I mentioned. The amount is in the order of S10 million or $15 million, of which the federal contribution would be only a portion, perhaps 25 per cent. The city of Toronto has agreed to contribute money, and the province will also be responsible for much of the expense.
If I may digress, Mr. Speaker, it may be remembered that the two national railways a few years ago proposed to rebuild completely Union Station, or relocate Union Station and some of the tracks. The proposal included the expansion of the station, which could accommodate increased traffic, and the rebuilding of the subway access. In other words, it was intended to rebuild a large transportation complex which would serve the needs of Torontonians for many years. The railways offered to do this at no cost to the taxpayers of Toronto, Ontario or Canada-all of which are the same people, if one wants to look at it that way. Unfortunately the objection of a
National Transportation Act
group of so-called radical reformers put this project in great jeopardy.
Toronto city council faced many difficulties. So many conditions were laid down, and so many complaints were raised about the project, that the railways finally said, "Forget it, we are not going to build metro centre. We will deny downtown Toronto this great revenue base which would include office buildings, apartment complexes and the new Massey Hall." The new hall was to be located in that general area as part of the project. Along with that went the promise of the railways to build a completely new transportation terminal for Toronto for next to nothing. I just mention that in passing.
If you read the newspapers, listen to television or the radio, you get the impression that it is just the federal government that is hampering the proper growth of transit services for commuters in Toronto. This, of course, is part of the Ontario government's tactic. They are in a very precarious position in the legislature, being attacked on all sides. They will use any ruse or argument for political gain. I suppose we have to understand their predicament, but we do not have to condone it.
It has been suggested, perhaps by the Minister of Transport and others, that a certain amount of the money which the Department of Transport- allocates to each province for such things as grade separation, railway relocation, and other normal statutory expenditures is used for other things. The minister says to Ontario, "Here is your money, this is what you are going to get." Ontario does not have to apply that to grade separations or railway relocations, whether it be in Niagara Falls, and I know there is a project contemplated there, or in Sudbury. If it prefers to apply the money to improve commuter services in and around Toronto, it has that flexibility. That is very generous of the minister. However, he should not tell his colleagues and this House that that would constitute some discharging of our responsibility with regard to assistance to urban and commuter transit. These are ongoing statutory problems that have nothing whatsoever to do with the promises made in 1974.
My colleague, the hon. member for Scarborough West (Mr. Martin), who is in the House today, has done a lot of work, together with the hon. member for Scarborough East (Mr. O'Connell) on the problem of grade separations. I am sure he will correct me if I am wrong. However, $20 million to $30 million could be spent on this one portion in the east end of metropolitan Toronto, the borough of Scarborough, to eliminate the grade separations. It is not really good form for the minister to say this is Ontario's money under statutory programs, but they can use it for commuter services and we will count that as discharging our promises to commuter transit. That argument just does not wash with me.
I am not issuing ultimatums but, like my colleague from Halton, there are some general requirements that I would like to see met by the government. My support for this bill is somewhat contingent upon their being met. I wish to reiterate them briefly.
3596

March 2, 1977
National Transportation Act
First, any federal financial assistance in the fields of urban or commuter transit must exclusively involve Canadian made systems and equipment. We have a pretty good record in this area. Hawker Siddeley of Thunder Bay have a world-wide reputation for making high speed, efficient, light subway trains. General Motors of Canada make most of the buses used by municipal transit systems. I believe they are built in London, Ontario. I am not sure whether the Western Flyer Company is still operating. In any event, they have received considerable orders from municipal transit systems over the past few years.
Second, all federal financial assistance must be allocated within specific time parameters. I touched on this earlier. The federal government cannot get itself into another open-ended spending program. It cannot just write a blank cheque for the provinces and municipalities to go on spending willy-nilly.
This has been done with very good intentions over the past ten or 20 years. We found that the provinces have not been responsible with the federal government's money. As I mentioned earlier, this was one of the main arguments for putting ceilings on medicare expenditures and the negotiation last November with the provinces to give them some of the tax points in return for them operating exclusively the medicare system. The federal financial commitments would not be forthcoming. They would get the money and spend it.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, will the hon. member permit a question at this time?

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO REDEFINE OBJECTIVE OF TRANSPORTATION POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Leggatt) is always kind and generous. With that kind and generous spirit, I am sure he will recognize that the hour is fast approaching six o'clock. There are other points I would like to make. If the hon. member will take the matter up with me privately, I will be very pleased to answer his questions.
Third, all federal financial assistance given to either Canadian Crown corporations and provincial or municipal transportation systems must receive full credit as an initiative made by the government of Canada. This cannot be regarded as a petty argument.
When dealing with provinces which routinely break faith in federal-provincial agreements it is absolutely necessary that the taxpayers of this country know which particular level of government is granting tax dollars in the field of urban transit, commuter transit, or whatever it may be. Too often moneys are given to the provinces, whether it be 25 per cent, 50 per cent or whatever, and the federal assistance is not acknowledged. Canadians should be informed that this is an initiative taken by the parliament of Canada.
There are other stipulations or suggestions I would make. Stipulations is a very pejorative term, of course. 1 will say suggestions. Federal Financial assistance to urban or commuter transit should pay for capital costs only, not operating costs. This is very important.
Finally, I would propose a re-adjustment of the formula outlined in June, 1974. I mentioned it earlier-25 per cent
[Mr. Collenette.)
toward the cost of urban vehicles and 100 per cent toward the cost of commuter vehicles. We should reduce the percentages somewhat.
If we are getting into a period of fixed funding for three or five years, we should scale down the original commitment. However, we should make some commitment. We cannot ignore the promise of assistance to urban and commuter transit acquisitions for municipalities or provinces. It cannot be completely ignored.
I would suggest 10 per cent toward the cost of urban vehicles, 25 per cent toward the cost of commuter vehicles, and 10 per cent toward the cost of new stations and platforms forming part of any commuter system. This is a reasonable compromise.
It was mentioned earlier that we do not have the money to expand urban systems. In the absolute sense that is true, because we are engaged in a period of restraint. However, there is a lot of money for a lot of other programs. I am not talking about those outside the Department of Transport. I would be loath to start chopping at other areas of government expenditures, certainly those I am not as familiar with as transport.
Having been a member of the Transport Committee since my election in 1974, it strikes me that an awful lot of the department's budget could bear further scrutiny. It was only a year and a half or two years ago that the government was prepared to spend $400 million on the Pickering airport. We know that figure was completely unrealistic in light of the final costs of Mirabel, which is rumoured to have cost more than $1 billion. We cannot get a straight figure on how much it costs.
In any event, the government was prepared to spend hundreds of millions of dollars on an airport that had not been fully justified. Sure, it was justified, I believe, by the Gibson inquiry, but many other critics have suggested that the building of a second airport in Toronto would be folly. Nevertheless, money was available at one time.
Money has been available to buy grain cars for the west. I do not want my colleagues from the west to take offence. I realize the government is in a bind. For decades governments in this country have failed to solve the basic problem posed by freight rate levels in western Canada. The railways cannot make a dollar hauling grain. The CP is a private company and I suppose it ought to make a profit. CN is not, but we want CN to make a profit if possible. And we have not been able to do anything but say, "We shall give you the money to buy hopper cars." However, in a rational transportation system the federal government would not be called upon to subsidize the means of conveying goods. These would be provided by the companies themselves.
This brings us to the question of fair tariffs, of fair freight rates, as well as a lot of questions affecting regional development. I know the minister is trying to tackle this aspect. I have been very critical of the government this afternoon but I should like to pay tribute to the minister. I do not agree with
March 2, 1977

him all the time. I know he has received some abuse this afternoon, and I am sure he has received abuse from his own colleagues from time to time. But he has devoted all his considerable mental powers to trying to rationalize the transportation system. I am not saying he has all the answers, but we have to give him credit for trying. For so long, successive governments have really been content to patch up the transportation system.
Where else is money available? I am sure that if I spent a few days, or a few weeks, looking over the transportation budget I could come up with lots more money. There is one example which comes to mind easily and which 1 see every week when I fly back to Toronto. It is the Five or six storey parking garage at Terminal Two. Someone has told me that this is costing $127.5 million, complete with infrastructure of roads and so on. That was just the initial cost, I was told; the final cost will be much higher than that. I think the minister would say it is costing only $40 million. I contend this is quite a large sum when we are thinking in terms of the $50 million mentioned by my hon. friend from Halton.
For too long this government and other governments before it have developed the air system in this country to the exclusion of all others. I agree that air travel is a force for national unity but we have the most highly subsidized, the most expensive airport system in the world. We built Mirabel. Mirabel, according to the minister, is the first airport which will be paid for by a revolving fund through user charges. I suppose this is the user-pay concept.
We have built Terminal One and Terminal Two in Toronto. I see the hon. member for Edmonton Centre (Mr. Paproski) in his place. We have built a fantastic airport in Edmonton. I was there last year. My God, when people from Alberta talk about neglect on the part of the federal government they should go to Edmonton Airport and see what the federal government has done for them. It is scandalous the expenditure which has been made there. And I am sure it is not even needed. Now I hear there is going to be further expansion in Calgary. So there is money available. All that is required is a reallocation of priorities.
I only have three or four minutes left, Mr. Speaker, and I really did want to talk about the rail passenger system. It is particularly appropriate I should do so in the light of the announcement made by the minister in Vancouver this week. 1 was one who supported the former minister of transport, Mr. Marchand, when he called for the creation of a public Canadian railway passenger corporation which would operate the services now operated by both railroads. I believe this is a forward step. I suppose that what the minister is proposing to do is to give directions to the Canadian Transport Commission to allow certain passenger services in this country to be phased out and replaced by limousines or bus services, the 80 per cent subsidy now paid under the National Transportation Act to be saved, and the money-I suppose it would be around $200 million a year-to form the basis of capital for the Via Canada system. speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to join in this debate. I am particularly interested in seeing the rag-tag group across the way calling themselves government supporters. As some of them know, they have been invited to come down and witness for themselves the congestion affecting public transport in Toronto on Monday, March 14, and I sincerely hope that in addition to standing up in the House and guardedly criticizing the government they will turn up on Monday morning, March 14, and start making some of the statements they have been making here today to the press as to how incompetent the government has been with respect to urban transit.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO REDEFINE OBJECTIVE OF TRANSPORTATION POLICY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speechtext:
I personnally invite not only those members opposite but the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald), and the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) to turn up and witness at first hand the congestion the government is leaving the commuter in the Toronto area to experience day in and day out. There are working people, the people who are paying the taxes which the federal treasury is mis-spending.
